svg.font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: GPT-6 Astra catches Claude Fable 5.1 for the number one spot in seven days without a new model shipping, because Artificial Analysis rewrote its Intelligence Index twice, and Astra's cost advantage at an identical list price comes from recurrent depth, the same architecture that reduced its chain-of-thought monitorability
svg.desc: A two-part figure covering September 5 to 20, 2026. On the left, three pairs of vertical bars compare Claude Fable 5.1 against OpenAI GPT-6 Astra on three successive versions of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, all within seven days and with no new model released between them. On Index version 4.1.1, used from September 1 to 3, Fable 5.1 scores 66 and Astra scores 61, a gap of 5 points. On version 4.2, published September 5, Fable scores 57 and Astra 55, a gap of 2 points. On version 4.3, published around September 7, both score 53, a gap of zero, and the number one position becomes a tie. A note warns that absolute scores fall with each re-weighting toward agentic work, so only the gap is comparable across versions, and that the y-axis is truncated. On the right, a callout headed same list price, less than half the bill explains that both models list at 10 dollars per million input tokens and 50 dollars per million output tokens, yet the measured cost to run the full Index is 3 dollars and 26 cents per task for Astra against 7 dollars and 63 cents for Fable 5.1, roughly 43 percent, so the entire cost advantage is token efficiency rather than price. Below it, a mechanism note states that Astra reportedly uses recurrent depth, also called looped transformers, which loops a shared stack of transformer blocks over a hidden state several times before emitting any token, so a large part of the reasoning happens in latent activations and never becomes readable text. This is why Astra emits fewer tokens and costs less, and it is also why OpenAI's own system card reports a substantial decrease in chain-of-thought monitorability compared with GPT-5.6 Sol, including shorter and sometimes empty chains of thought. Efficiency and opacity are the same mechanism. A footer records a second effect of the re-weighting: the more agentic ruler widened rather than narrowed the gap between open and closed models. Under version 4.1.1 the leading open weights models GLM-5.3 and Kimi K3 scored 60 against the top closed score of 66, a gap of 6 points; under version 4.3 they score 44 against 53, a gap of 9 points.
svg.text: #1 becomes a TIE in seven days — because the RULER moved, not the models
No new frontier model shipped between these three points. Artificial Analysis re-weighted the Intelligence Index toward agentic work twice.
Claude Fable 5.1 (Sep 1) vs GPT-6 Astra (Sep 3) — same two models, three rulers
Absolute scores deflate with each re-weighting — only the GAP is comparable. Y-axis truncated.

The same re-weighting WIDENED the open-vs-closed gap — agentic work is where open weights lose most
Under v4.1.1: open leaders GLM-5.3 and Kimi K3 at 60 vs the top closed score of 66 → gap 6
Under v4.3: the same two at 44 vs the tied top of 53 → gap 9 (GLM-5.3-Flash 42 · Qwen3.8 2.4T 40 · DeepSeek V4 Pro 36)
Through-line: the frontier "split" of Sep-05 did not persist as two rankings — the measurement layer absorbed it,
and the tie it produced rests on an architecture whose efficiency and whose opacity are one and the same thing.
Scores: Artificial Analysis (third party). Architecture: reported by The Information, not confirmed by OpenAI. Monitorability decline: OpenAI's own system card.
